title: Optical time travel: proposal for testing Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture in an optical analogue
abstract: Classical general relativity allows time travel, but Hawking [Phys. Rev. D 46, 603 (1992)] conjectured that quantum mechanics ultimately prevents it. Here we propose a feasible experiment to test Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture in optics. In this scheme, time travel is inherently related to lasing, and the amplified vacuum fluctuations above laser threshold establish the quantum limits of time travel
summary: The paper outlines an experimental proposal to test Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture using an optical time machine built from a fiber loop and parametric amplifier. By analyzing both classical and full quantum field dynamics, the authors show that while time travel is classically possible under high gain, quantum noise generation fundamentally limits or prevents it.
main_problem: The paper proposes an optical analogue experiment to test Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture (CPC), which suggests quantum mechanics prevents time travel.
main_result: While classical analysis suggests that time travel is possible under conditions of high gain exceeding loss, the quantum mechanical treatment predicts that vacuum fluctuations will generate measurable extra noise, thereby imposing limitations on any achievable time machine.
method: The authors use both classical differential equation solving (Fourier transforms) and full quantum field quantization techniques (mode operators, Wigner functions) to model light propagation through an amplifier feedback loop.
model_or_system: The system is an optical setup involving a fiber connected to a loop via a parametric amplifier ($\chi^{(2)}$ crystal), designed to mimic the closed null geodesics required for time travel in general relativity.
key_observables: Classical fidelity ($F$), extra quantum noise quantified by particle number ($ ar{n}$), and the temporal relationship between input and output pulses.
important_parameters: Amplifier gain parameter ($\zeta$), loss parameter ($\gamma$), and the time delay in the loop ($t_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that quantum noise generation (amplification of vacuum fluctuations) is the dominant effect, and it compares regimes where classical causality might be violated versus where quantum constraints must hold.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spacetime diagram for time travel, the optical setup using a fiber loop/parametric amplifier, and temporal comparisons showing output pulses preceding input arrivals.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical link between GR time travel and amplified vacuum fluctuations (Hawking's argument), developing classical solutions for light propagation in the ring, and finally quantizing the system to calculate the unavoidable quantum noise associated with the process.
why_interesting: This work bridges general relativity concepts (closed timelike curves) directly into the domain of quantum optics and open quantum systems by using parametric amplification as a physical model for vacuum energy buildup.

(7) and (8)] compared with −a1(t + t0) [grey curve] for a gain of 10 (cosh2 ζ = 10) and no loss. Only the envelopes of the pulses are shown (for their optical oscillations see Fig. 5). The separate plot in blue shows the initial light in the loop [Eqs. (2) and (8)]. As input pulse we took a1 = A sech[−10(t −1.25 t0)/t0)] where the bulk of the incident pulse arrives in the interval [t0, 2t0]. We clearly see that the output leaves before the input has arrived, and with good fidelity (80%, see Appendix B) even for modest gain.

Figure 3: Box modes. We quantize the field in terms of box modes (boxes, labeled by integers) that are long in comparison with the wavelength and short in comparison with the variations of the pulse amplitudes (red). The modes interact with each other at the amplifier (dot).

Figure 4: Setup. Our scheme (Fig. 1) can be implemented in free–space optics using a χ(2) crystal41 as parametric amplifier24 (grey box). The signal mode of the amplifier serves as the signal in our setup, with amplitudes a1 before and b1 after amplification. The idler,24 with amplitudes a0 before and b0 after amplification, is reflected by mirrors to form the loop of the optical time machine (Fig. 1).
